newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Waigel, facing budget crisis, skips G7 summit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Waigel, facing budget crisis, skips G7 summit.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, under pressure to end a budget crisis that has shaken the ruling coalition, will skip this week's Group of Seven (G7) economic summit, the finance ministry said on Monday.

Rather than attend the splashy June 20-22 summit of leaders from the world's richest industrial nations, Waigel will stay home to put his own house in order as Germany frantically tries to qualify for Europe's planned single currency.

"It is important for the minister to clear up pressing questions of growth and employment at home," a finance ministry spokesman said. "There are a number of things to talk about in the next few days, including the budgets for 1997 and 1998."

Waigel's decision to stay home is fresh evidence of the unabated crisis within Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition of Christian Democrats (CDU) and Free Democrats (FDP) that has brought the 14-year-old government close to the breaking point.
Stubbornly high unemployment and weak economic growth have caused tax revenues to fall sharply and ripped huge holes in far too optimistic budgets for 1997 and 1998.
Desperate to fill widening budget deficits, the CDU and the FDP have clashed over how to carry out an income tax reform that would lower tax burdens on individuals and businesses.

Waigel needs to fill the revenue gap in order to stop the deficit from ballooning beyond three percent of gross domestic product as required by monetary union criteria and has mulled raising petrol or value added taxes.

But the tax-cutting FDP have vowed to their voters not to accept any tax increases to patch the budget, putting the government in the position of making more unpopular spending cuts or finding another way to fill the budget gap.
And they have to do it soon.
Waigel is under pressure to come up with a basic outline of the 1998 budget and is expected to present a supplementary budget raising the new borrowing target for 1997 by June 25.
That is the date of the next meeting of the financial planning council -- a group of federal and state government and central bank financial experts.

Then the proposals must wind their way through two weeks of gruelling inter-party negotiations and will be presented to the federal cabinet on July 11 and voted on in parliament in the second half of September.
The government's increasingly less-ambitious tax reform will be presented to parliament on June 26.
Bonn's fiscal woes have become one of the key uncertainties that could derail Europe's ambitious goal of establishing a single currency in 1999.

Adamantly opposed to any tax increases, FDP leader Wolfgang Gerhardt has said it might be necessary to raise the federal deficit this year, which could make it more difficult for Bonn to meet the EMU deficit target.

"This might work for the 1997 budget in order to overcome these acute difficulties," said Gerhardt in an interview with the Saechsische Zeitung to appear on Tuesday. "But debt must really be kept within limits in 1998."
